content:
There's a factory in Hsinchu, Taiwan, that you've never heard of and that your life depends on. It's run by the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, and it makes most of the world's advanced microchips. The processor in your phone was almost certainly fabricated there. So were the chips in your car, your laptop, the servers running your bank, and the systems managing air traffic control and power grids and hospital equipment - a staggering share of them, from fabs on an island of twenty-four million people in the western Pacific.

I find the achievement itself genuinely moving, and I think we should sit with it for a moment before getting to the problem. We've worked out how to lay down circuitry a few atoms wide, hundreds of billions of times, on a wafer of purified sand, with an error rate low enough that the thing boots. It is probably the most refined manufacturing process our species has ever managed, and almost nobody outside the industry could name the company that does it.

The shortage disrupting global industry this year has made the dependency visible in a way it wasn't before. Car manufacturers have stopped production lines. Electronics companies have delayed launches. Prices have risen across the vast category of things that contain a chip, which is now very nearly everything.

The shortage is the small problem. The geography is the large one.

**A Single Point of Failure**

Taiwan sits about 160 kilometres from mainland China, which considers the island part of its sovereign territory. The United States maintains strategic ambiguity about defending it, neither committing nor ruling it out. The military balance in the strait has been moving in China's favour for decades. The most critical supply chain on earth runs through the most contested strait on earth, and I haven't yet found anyone with a credible plan for what happens if it closes.

This isn't Hormuz, and the difference matters. Oil has substitutes and they're improving every year. If Hormuz shut tomorrow the disruption would be severe and the world would adapt, because the commodity moving through it is already being superseded.

Advanced semiconductors have no substitute and no second source. Intel is trying to rebuild American capacity and is years from the cutting edge. Samsung has fabs in Korea that don't match TSMC at the most advanced nodes. A leading-edge fab costs upwards of twenty billion dollars, takes five years, and needs an ecosystem of lithography suppliers, materials chemistry and several thousand engineers who've done it before. Price signals don't conjure any of that on the timeline a crisis would demand.

And a crisis wouldn't require a war. A blockade would do it. A quarantine zone. Any posture that made shipping into Taiwanese ports uninsurable. The fabs wouldn't need to be touched - only made unreachable. Within weeks the supply of advanced chips would begin to constrict, and within months production of everything downstream would slow or stop. What worries me most is that the cascade is genuinely hard to model, because that tells you the dependencies are pervasive enough that nobody has finished mapping them.

For Australia the position is stark. We have no semiconductor industry, no fabrication capability and no path to one. The chips in our infrastructure, our defence systems, our communications networks and our economy all come from somewhere else, and if that somewhere else becomes unreachable we have no domestic substitute and no timeline for building one.

**What We Should Actually Do About It**

We're not going to have a leading-edge fab, and I'd rather say that plainly than watch another decade of announcements pretending otherwise. We don't have the engineers, the ecosystem or the market, and a country of twenty-six million chasing a twenty-billion-dollar facility is a way of spending money to feel busy.

What we can do is finish the audit nobody has finished. We do not currently know, with any precision, which Australian systems fail first if advanced chips stop arriving - in what order, on what timeline, and which specific components are involved. Not chips in general. The actual part numbers inside water treatment control systems, grid management, hospital equipment and telecommunications. That work is unglamorous, costs almost nothing against any defence line item, and would give us the one thing we completely lack right now, which is a list.

A list changes what's possible. Once you know it's four thousand components rather than four million, holding a year of strategic inventory stops being absurd and becomes a procurement decision. Once you know which systems fail first, you can decide which of them are worth hardening. And once the list exists it can be maintained, which means the position stops depending on whichever official last thought about it.

Beyond that, we should treat allied fab construction as our own infrastructure. Arizona, Kumamoto and Dresden are more relevant to Australian resilience than most projects inside our borders, and our industrial policy should say so and put money behind it - equity, offtake agreements, research partnerships, and a serious position in the parts of the chain that actually suit us, which is materials, rare earths, specialist packaging and the power to run all of it.

None of this is an argument for decoupling. The chips flow today and the goal isn't to stop them. The goal is to make sure their flowing isn't the only thing holding the economy upright.

**The Concentration Wasn't a Plot**

I've been to Taiwan. It's a remarkable place - democratic, prosperous, technically sophisticated, culturally alive - and the people I met live with a strategic uncertainty that would paralyse most societies. They understand their own vulnerability far better than anyone lecturing them about it, and they're the last people who need this explained.

It's worth being clear that Hsinchu happened because a company became genuinely the best in the world at something and every customer made the sensible individual choice to buy from the best. There's nobody to blame here and no decision to reverse. That's precisely why efficiency won't fix it: the same logic that produced the concentration will keep producing it, one rational contract at a time, until something interrupts.

So it has to be built deliberately, at cost, by people willing to pay for redundancy that looks unnecessary right up until the morning it's the only thing that matters. We built a civilisation on one island without ever deciding to. Building a second, and a third, is a decision still entirely open to us - and unlike most strategic problems, we can see this one coming clearly, years out, with time to act.
